summary: This experimental RFC proposes a change to DKIM that lets a domain advertise authorizations for third-party signatures, to be treated as equivalent to a signature added by the author's own administrative domain.

eli5.summary: Normally a letter is stamped by its sender's company. This experiment lets the company say another trusted company may stamp it on its behalf and have it count the same.

questions: how does third party dkim signing work
subtitle: Authorizing third-party services to sign email with DKIM on a domain's behalf

tldr.problem: DKIM signatures normally only count as trustworthy when the signing domain matches the email's From: header domain. But many organizations use third-party email services (like marketing platforms) that want to sign emails on their behalf. The services either need their own private keys or access to the domain's keys, both creating security and operational headaches.
tldr.mechanism: ATPS (Authorized Third-Party Signatures) lets a domain publish a DNS record authorizing specific third-party services to add DKIM signatures that count as equivalent to a signature from the domain itself. The third-party signer includes special tags in its DKIM signature, and the receiver verifies the authorization by querying the domain's DNS.
tldr.outcome: Third-party email services can sign messages without possessing domain private keys or signing on behalf of arbitrary domains. Email receivers can trust these signatures as equivalent to domain-authenticated messages. The approach remains experimental; most deployments still use traditional DKIM or key delegation.

today: RFC 6541 remains Experimental. It is implemented in at least two email security systems but is not widely deployed. Organizations often use simpler alternatives like traditional DKIM key delegation or separate signing by third parties. If operational experience shows ATPS reduces the complexity and security issues of third-party signing, it could be elevated to Standards Track. The main challenge remains DNS query latency in high-volume mail systems.

sections.title: The Third-Party Signing Problem
sections.content:
DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) lets a domain cryptographically sign emails to prove they came from that domain. The signature works best when the signing domain matches the email's From: header—this gives the highest level of trust. But when a company uses a third-party email service (like a marketing platform or email delivery service), that service needs to sign the mail somehow.

Normally, there are only two bad options: give the third party access to the domain's private keys (a security risk) or have the third party sign with its own domain (which looks less trustworthy). RFC 6541 introduces ATPS—a way for the domain to announce that a specific third party is authorized to sign on its behalf, so the third party's signature counts as equivalent to a signature from the domain itself.
sections.eli5: When a company uses a mailing service, that service needs to sign emails in a way that the company's customers will trust. ATPS lets the company tell everyone 'My mailing service can stamp mail on my behalf.'

sections.title: How ATPS Works
sections.content:
An ATPS Signer (the third-party service) adds two new tags to the DKIM signature it creates: an atps tag containing the domain it is signing on behalf of, and an atpsh tag naming the hash algorithm used for DNS lookups. When a receiver gets the message, it validates the DKIM signature normally. If the signature is valid and has an atps tag, the receiver queries DNS to check whether the domain announced this authorization.

The domain publishes the authorization as a TXT record in DNS. To avoid name collisions when many services are authorized, the service's domain is hashed (using SHA-1 or SHA-256) and converted to base32, then the record is queried under a special subdomain. If the DNS record exists, the receiver treats the third-party signature as equivalent to a signature from the domain itself.
sections.eli5: The signing service writes 'I am signing this on behalf of example.com' in the signature. The receiver asks the DNS: 'Did example.com authorize me to do this?' If DNS says yes, the receiver trusts it.

sections.title: DNS Query Construction
sections.content:
To query whether a third party is authorized, the receiver constructs a DNS TXT query using this process: (1) extract the signer's domain from the DKIM signature's d= tag, (2) hash it using the algorithm named in the atpsh tag, (3) convert the hash output to base32 (a safe encoding for DNS), and (4) append the string ._atps. followed by the domain from the atps tag. For example, if the signer is mail.service.com with SHA-1 hashing and it is authorized by example.com, the query would look like QSP4I4D24CRHOPDZ3O3ZIU2KSGS3X6Z6._atps.example.com.

If a valid ATPS record exists, it contains a version tag (which must be ATPS1) and optionally a plain-text copy of the signer's domain for collision detection. The plaintext domain is included as a safeguard in case the base32 encoding produces a collision with another authorized signer.
sections.eli5: The receiver hashes the signer's name, converts it to base32, and asks DNS: 'Is THISHASH._atps.example.com a real record?' If yes, the authorization is confirmed.

sections.title: Interpretation and Trust
sections.content:
When ATPS confirms an authorization, the receiver SHOULD treat the third-party signature as if the domain itself had signed the message. This means reputation systems and filtering rules that normally apply to the domain should also apply to third-party signatures. For example, if example.com has a good reputation, a message signed by an authorized service will inherit that reputation.

ATPS also interacts with ADSP (Author Domain Signing Practices), another DKIM extension that lets domains specify policies about unsigned mail. If both are implemented, ATPS MUST be checked first; if ATPS confirms the signature, the message is treated as having a valid author signature for ADSP purposes.
sections.eli5: Once the domain authorizes a service, that service's signature is treated as trustworthy as the domain's own signature. Any good reputation the domain has carries over to messages signed by the authorized service.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A domain that authorizes a third party takes on the risk that the third party becomes compromised. If a malicious actor gains control of an authorized service, they can sign spam or phishing emails using the domain's reputation, causing severe damage. Domains MUST carefully vet and continuously monitor any third party they authorize.

The hashing and base32 encoding used in DNS queries is NOT a security mechanism. They exist only to convert arbitrary domain names to fixed-width DNS labels. The obscuration provides no real privacy; the point is to make the relationship discoverable by anyone who needs to verify it. Also, weak hash algorithms like SHA-1 carry collision risk, so domains SHOULD prefer SHA-256 when possible.
sections.eli5: If you authorize a service and it gets hacked, the hacker can send bad mail with your signature. You need to watch your authorized services closely. The hashing is just for convenience; it does not hide anything.

sections.title: Current Status and Limitations
sections.content:
ATPS remains Experimental. It has been implemented in at least two software products (one open source, widely used), but it is not deployed at the same scale as standard DKIM. One concern is the load on DNS: a receiver checking ATPS, ADSP, and multiple DKIM signatures may issue many parallel DNS queries, creating latency and potential bottlenecks during mail delivery.

The RFC suggests an alternative using HTTPS instead of DNS to reduce DNS load, but this would require the domain to operate a web server and adds other security considerations. Most production deployments still use traditional key delegation or have the third party sign with its own domain. ATPS provides a valuable option for organizations that want tighter control over third-party signing authority.
sections.eli5: Some companies use this method, and it is built into email security software. But it is not as common as simpler methods because DNS lookups can be slow. If the experiment goes well, it might become a standard someday.
